cards.front: How does comparing two genome sequences reveal genetic differences between people?
cards.back: Computers line up the sequences and find positions where the **bases do not match**. These mismatches show differences such as SNPs or different alleles.
cards.hint: Think about lining up two copies of the same text and spotting letters that differ.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to think that carrying a risk allele means a person will definitely get the disease?
cards.back: A risk allele only changes the **probability** of disease. It does not guarantee illness, because diet, lifestyle and other genes also matter.
Using an individual's **genetic information** to choose treatments, doses or preventive measures suited to that person.
cards.hint: Think about what a doctor starts from when planning care for one person.

cards.back: One of two or more alternative versions of the same **gene**.

cards.front: What is a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)?
cards.back: A position in the genome where a **single base** differs between individuals.
cards.hint: Ask how many bases differ at that position.

cards.front: How can different alleles lead to two people clearing the same drug at different speeds?
cards.back: Alleles can alter the **molecules that break the drug down**, so one person clears it quickly and another clears it slowly.
cards.hint: Think about what alleles code for and what the body does to a drug first.

cards.front: How is the warfarin dose tailored to a patient?
cards.back: It is adjusted to the person's **alleles** that affect how the drug is broken down.
cards.hint: Compare this with giving every patient the same fixed dose.

cards.front: Why is trastuzumab given to some breast cancer patients but not others?
cards.back: It is given only if the tumour tests positive, because tumour cells make large amounts of the **HER2 receptor**.
cards.hint: Think about which test the tumour must pass before treatment starts.

cards.front: Why does tailoring treatment to genes improve care?
cards.back: It can make a treatment work better and spares people who would gain no benefit or would suffer **harm** from the drug.
The **unfair treatment** of a person because of their genetic information, for example by insurers or employers.
cards.hint: Think about who might see a person's genetic results.

cards.front: Why might access to personalised medicine be unequal?
cards.back: Sequencing and tailored drugs can be **expensive**, so some patients may be left out.
cards.hint: Think about who has to pay for the testing and the drugs.

cards.front: Why do most differences in genome sequences have no effect on health?
cards.back: Much of the genome does not code for protein, and many base changes inside genes do not alter the protein, so researchers must find which differences **matter**.
cards.hint: Think about which parts of DNA actually make proteins.
